Managing process templates is an administrative function, so the Manage Process Templates app appears under the Administrator group in the SAP Fiori launchpad, whereas the Manage Process app is under General Planner .

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: The process participants, process owners, and reviewers use this app to view the status of the process. SAP IBP provides the business authorization to control the user’s access to perform view or edit actions in the Manage Process Template or Manage Processes apps. Before creating a process template, there are a few organizational questions that need to be answered Who are the owners of the process template? In general, the S&OP process owner is responsible for the managing the process. There can be more than one owner of a process.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: What process steps need to be included in each template? Typically, the S&OP process includes five process steps, as mentioned at the beginning of the chapter. However, some regions/countries may have di ff erent process steps and cadence. For example, in the US monthly S&OP process, there could be five steps, whereas the Canadian S&OP process may have four steps starting with demand review (i.e., the product review process could be part of the demand review). © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 325 What is the duration of each process step? In a monthly S&OP process, the goal is to start the processes at the beginning of month and end during the last week with a management business review. Therefore, each S&OP process step is about three to five days in duration— sometimes less and sometimes more. Are the process steps sequential or parallel? S&OP process steps are usually sequential; however, you can model parallel process steps in an S&OP process. For example, in the Canada S&OP process template, the process step for demand review could be split into two parallel steps—sales review and demand review—with some overlapping dates.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Who are the owners and participants in each step? It’s common for each process step to have a di ff erent process step owner to manage its lifecycle. There can be one or more participant groups in a process step. For example, in the US S&OP template, for the demand review step, there can be three participant groups: US sales planners, US demand planners, and US marketing planners. What are the tasks that need to be executed during a process step and by whom? During each process stage, there are several tasks that need to be executed by the planners.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: For example, during the demand review phase, sales planners need to enter the sales forecast, the sales director needs to approve the forecast, and marketing managers need to enter promotions and pricing information, and so on. These tasks need to be completed to move to the next stage of the process. Is automation required for the process steps? Process steps can be automated to always start on a certain date, start when the previous step is completed, end when all tasks are completed, and so on. What batch processes should be included in the automation?

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Sometimes, certain batch jobs can be associated with a process step’s start or end state. For example, when a demand review step starts, you may want to run the statistical forecast, or when the management business review ends, run the copy operation and perform a data integration outbound job for SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA. Once these questions have been answered for a process template, the process template owner can create the required templates in SAP IBP. The next section Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 327 9.2 Setting Up Process Templates and Automations The Manage Process Templates app shows a list of all available templates created, as shown in Figure 9.2. For example, the US, Canada, Mexico, and Eastern and Northwestern S&OP templates are visible in this list when created. This list view also provides the capability to start a process or quickly copy an existing process template to create a new one. Figure 9.2 Process Template List View As shown in Figure 9.3, within the process template, a list of process steps created is provided, along with a Gantt chart view showing the steps overview.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: This allows the process owner a quick view of the process steps, their duration, and whether there are any overlapping steps, along with the automation criteria. The circles indicate that there are SAP IBP application jobs associated with the step, and arrows show whether there are any automation criteria defined for each step. The following sections cover all the relevant areas of the process template in detail with examples of their usage and setup. We start with the process roles, time zones, and weekday settings, followed by detailed settings of process steps, tasks assignments, process step automations, and process orchestration of application jobs, and finally cover the visualizations of the process template with Gantt charts.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 328 Figure 9.3 SAP IBP Process Template 9.2.1 Process Roles As shown previously in Figure 9.3, process templates also show the process owners, participant groups, and reviewers associated with each process step. Because SAP IBP manages collaboration across various functional groups, it’s important that the right groups of users are assigned to the right process steps. For example, a demand review participant group for the demand review step is a user group consisting of demand planners in the United States. This can be set up in the User Groups section of SAP IBP.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Typically, participants in the process step are assigned tasks. There can be one or more participant groups for a process. For example, the product and portfolio review step may have two user groups, consisting of product management and marketing planners. Other than the participant groups, there can be reviewers assigned to a process step, who are involved within a process step and monitor the status but don’t perform tasks in that step. For example, in a supply review step, the demand planners and financial planners can act as reviewers: they’re involved in the progress of the process but not performing any activities within the process. 9.2.2 Time Zone, Workday, and Duration Settings for Process Steps When the S&OP process is managed globally with several regional- and country- specific processes, the time zones and local times are considered by SAP IBP process management.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: This ensures that the processes are running and the tasks are assigned correctly according to the local time zone settings of the process. In the running example, if you have two processes—US S&OP and Eastern Europe © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 329 S&OP—you want to ensure that the right time zones are assigned to each so that the automation settings with respect to scheduling application jobs associated with the process or starting/ending the process and assignment of tasks adhere to this setting. SAP IBP process management also provides settings for default workdays, as shown in Figure 9.4—for example, for work weeks starting on Monday and ending on Friday each week. These settings are used when creating a process for this template for each month; the template automatically considers the work days for each process step.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Figure 9.4 Localized Time Zone and Workday Settings for Process Template In a template, you only define the duration of each process step. When creating a process, the actual dates are calculated considering the step duration and workdays. 9.2.3 Tasks Assignment A set of template tasks can be defined for each planning step. Usually in a planning process step, di ff erent activities are happening, and the participant users are responsible for the timely completion of those activities. Figure 9.5 shows a demand review step in which di ff erent plans are created and consolidated to reach a consensus demand plan considering the assumptions for the demand changes.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: In the demand review meeting, this plan is reviewed and approved, along with capturing action items and new sets of assumptions. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 330 Figure 9.5 Sample Demand Review Process Activities In SAP IBP, one or more tasks can be defined for a process step and assigned to participant groups and/or users associated with that process step. Task management in SAP IBP will be covered in more detail later in Section 9.4, where we’ll discuss how tasks are assigned to users, how they are monitored and completed, how to create ad hoc tasks, and more. For example, a demand review step may have a task called Update Sales Forecasts, which is assigned to a participant group, US Sales Planners.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Assume that there are 100 sales planners in the United States. When the process step starts, this single task is then set up as 100 individual SAP Build Work Zone tasks and assigned to each sales planner. Users get notifications when tasks are assigned, and as they complete the tasks, the step progress increases. There is no order sequence for the tasks. All tasks will follow the same duration as the step duration and will start and end based on the step dates. As shown in Figure 9.6, for each process step, one or more tasks are assigned.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Figure 9.6 shows the flexible layout for process steps, which increases the ability to view the di ff erent process steps and jump to the header and details of each process step. The left part of the flexible layout is the Steps overview, showing the step list and Gantt chart. For each step selected, the right side shows the details of the step: participation, duration, automation settings, job templates, and tasks. In SAP IBP process templates, you can also create process steps without tasks. Examples of this functionality include the following: Process steps that represent a milestone within the process, like the process step for the management review that concludes a process Process steps that have application jobs assigned and that are configured to run automatically © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 331 Figure 9.6 Tasks and Automation Settings for Template 9.2.4 Process Steps Automation As shown previously in Figure 9.6, the process template owner can assign automation criteria for how the steps should start and end. In the example, the demand review step starts when the previous step, product and portfolio review, is completed; the step ends when the tasks associated with the demand review step are completed—that is, when all tasks are completed, and the progress reaches 100%. Note that the process owner can explicitly define the previous step for the current step.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: For example, the demand planning step can be defined with the previous step’s settings such as sales planning and marketing planning. If the previous step isn’t defined, the system uses the chronological order to determine the previous step. SAP IBP provides the flexibility to customize the automation criteria for each process step. As mentioned earlier, the step automations can be defined for the start and/or end steps. The default is to not have automation; that is, start and end are activated manually by the step owner.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: When you select automation criteria, you have several options. For the start step, the standard conditions are On Start Date , When Previous Step Is Completed , When End Application Job of Previous Step Is Completed , or No Custom Alerts at End of Previous Step . Similar settings are o ff ered for the end condition: On End Date , When Tasks Are Completed (this selection is only available when SAP Build Work Zone is enabled), or When Start Application Job Is Completed or No Custom Alerts at Start of Step . You can choose one or more of these conditions and apply conditions for the selection.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 332 For example, the start condition of the process step can be defined as follows: to start on the start date and when the ending job of the previous step is completed, as shown in Figure 9.7. This can be the case for, say, an integrated reconciliation step in which you always start on the 16th day of each month, but only when its previous step (supply review) is completed based on the completion of that step’s end application job (e.g., a copy operator). Figure 9.7 Process Step Automation Settings Other conditions can be set such that the management business review meetings always start on their set start date and end on the end date irrespective of the status completions of the prior steps.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Therefore, process automation provides the flexibility to define the automation criteria for each step, and this can be di ff erent across di ff erent process templates. For example, the US process template may have demand review start as soon as the product review step is completed, whereas in the Canada S&OP process, the demand review step may have a criterion to always start on the start date. Note that the automation criteria can be manually overridden; for example, the process step owner can choose to complete the process earlier, thus overriding the automation criterion for that step to end on its end date.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Process automation in SAP Integrated Business Planning for sales and operations allows you to manage processes based on exceptions. Custom alert subscriptions can be assigned to process steps at the starting or ending stage of the step. You can further define automation criteria on how the process should progress when alerts are detected. If you set up the automation criteria based on alerts, the process step won’t proceed to the next stage if there are alerts present on the execution of the custom alerts associated with the step.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 333 address these alerts or manually set the process step to the next stage. Examples of process automation based on alerts include the following: The demand planning process step should not start if an alert is raised for actuals quantity having no values. The supply planning process step should not start if there is an alert raised where demand plan accuracy is less than 85%. The supply planning process step should not finish if there are capacity overload alerts. Custom alert subscriptions assigned to process steps can be configured for visibility of alerts and/or to control process automations.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Alerts are triggered when the process step is started or ended. The subsequent step won’t start until the alerts are resolved (depending on automation criteria). There may be cases where issues identified by a custom alert may not be critical enough to interrupt the process. Nevertheless, you may want to be made aware of these issues. For example, before you do demand planning, you want to check that the key figure values for the sales history actuals don’t have any null values in past time periods. In this case, you can add a custom alert that checks the data, but you don’t choose a condition for the automatic start or end of the process step.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: If an alert is triggered, the alert will be shown for the process step, but the process isn’t stopped. When alerts occur as part of process step execution, you can see the count of alerts associated with each of the alert subscriptions in the process step details. From there, you can navigate to the custom alert definition or to the alerts in the Monitor Custom Alerts app. SAP Integrated Business Planning for sales and operations lets you define exception conditions based on certain user-defined criteria, especially when there is an AND condition for the steps.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: For example, a supply review step can be configured in such a way to only end once its end date has been reached and when tasks are completed; if there is an exception, then an exception state can be defined by the user as Delayed . This is a configurable field in the process settings. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 334 9.2.5 Process Orchestration of Application Jobs As part of a monthly process cycle, there can be many batch jobs that need to run. For example, when the step starts, you may want to clear the key figures to be ready for planning. When the demand review step begins, you may want to run a statistical forecast job, or when the final plan is confirmed, run a snapshot operator or copy operators. SAP IBP provides the ability to run application jobs as part of Excel and in the Application Jobs app. In addition, to orchestrate process-oriented scheduling of application jobs in which the application jobs are run not just based on dates but also based on the automation criteria of the steps, these application job templates can be associated with a process step.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: The step settings let you assign only one application job setting per start and end of the step. In Figure 9.8, for the US demand review step, we’ve assigned an application job template for when the step ends. Figure 9.8 Parallel Process Steps When a process owner manually sets a step to complete, the application job associated with the end step is immediately triggered. The same is true if the process step ends when the automation criteria is reached. Typically, the processes owner defines the application job templates that need to be assigned to a step.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: In the example, there are five process templates, one for each country/subregion. For each of the demand review end steps, we can assign a country- or subregion-specific custom application job template. These application job templates will run based on the process cadence. In Section 9.3, we’ll further discuss how the application jobs are run, their authorizations, and automation criteria. © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 335 9.2.6 Gantt Chart View of Sequential and Parallel Processes Gantt charts provide process owners with a good visual overview of the automation associated with each step. Here, a process step with no automation will have no directional arrows. In Figure 9.8, the process shows two parallel steps: sales and marketing review and demand review. The dates overlap, such that the sales step ends before the demand review step. The circle next to the demand review indicates that there’s an application job associated with the end step of the demand review process, and the process bar shows that there are start and end step automations associated with the demand review step.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: With such a setup, the process owner can quickly understand the overall step dependencies and adjust the settings as needed. Another capability o ff ered by process management is making certain key figures editable only when a process stage is active or the process step dates have been reached. The process steps in the process template have settings to assign permission filters to participants/participant groups. When the process step is in progress, the permission filters are applied to the users; when the step is completed, these permissions are removed, thereby e ff ecting the key figure editability for users.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: This topic is covered in Chapter 15 in more detail. So far, we’ve discussed how to create process templates for di ff erent countries and subregions. Next, we’ll discuss how to create monthly recurring processes from these templates and how to visualize and monitor the processes. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 336 9.3 Manage Processes The Manage Processes app provides process monitoring, visualization, and lifecycle management for S&OP processes. Based on their assigned user role, a user can be an owner, participant, or reviewer of a process step. There are three important aspects of managing processes, which we’ll discuss in detail: Create one or more process instances. Manage the lifecycle of the process. View and monitor the status of the process. In this section, we’ll provide an overview of what a process is and then walk you through creating a process.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: We’ll then discuss managing and monitoring processes. 9.3.1 What Is a Process? A process is an instance of a process template that runs every recurring period. For example, for the US S&OP template, there can be one process for each month: January 2022 US S&OP process, February 2022 US S&OP Process, and so on. As shown in Figure 9.9, each process has actual dates associated with it, and its steps based on the duration and workdays are defined in the template. Figure 9.9 Processes for Process Template The Manage Processes app shows a list view of all the processes on entry with a clear indication of the running processes, closed processes, and processes that are overdue.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 337 processes list view shown in Figure 9.10 shows the processes that are overdue and indicates the overall process status completion and if there are any exceptions to the process (e.g., the start date was reached, and the previous step isn’t completed). A quick overview of the current running steps also is shown. In our example, one or more processes can be defined for each of the process templates, but typically only one process will be running, and others will be closed or not yet started. Figure 9.10 Process List Overview for Process Monitoring Processes in SAP IBP have only three statuses: Open , Overdue , or Closed .

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: The Overdue status indicates that the days remaining for the process is zero or the current date is past the process end date. 9.3.2 Creating a Process In the Manage Processes app, processes can be created for each process template. The only information that needs to be provided is the process name, start date of the process, and any adjustments to the dates. For the sample template, you can define processes for the next planning cycle or as required for the next six months of the planning cycle. When a process instance is created for the process, you can specify a default start date; all other dates of the process steps are adjusted considering the duration of the step and the workdays, based on the default start date set.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: For example, if a process step starts on Friday and has a duration of four days, then the dates of the process step will be adjusted such that the four days excludes the nonworking days (i.e., Saturday and Sunday); thereby the end date becomes Wednesday of the following week. If there are any fiscal holidays for the region in which the process is run, then they need to be taken into account and the dates adjusted manually for the process step start and end dates along with the dates of the other steps. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 338 In addition to the dates, the process step owner can choose to enter the start date and time if step automation is included with date-based criteria, as shown in Figure 9.11. For example, you can choose to have the step start at 9 a.m. in the time zone setting of the process so that any application jobs are run at that time, and any tasks are created for the users at 9 a.m. The management business review process step has automation settings to start on the start date with a start time of 9 a.m. and end on the end date with an end time of 6 p.m.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: When the process step is completed at 6 p.m., the Copy Final Constrained Plan job will be triggered immediately. Figure 9.11 Process Settings for Dates and Times Process owners can create more than one process for a template (January US S&OP, February US S&OP, etc.). If there are automation settings for the processes defined such that the processes start on a defined date, then these processes will be automatically executed by the system sequentially. 9.3.3 Managing Process Lifecycle After the processes have been created from a process instance, they’re automatically run when automation criteria are defined for the steps.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: You can also manually run the process steps for steps that don’t have automation defined for them. The process steps have a lifecycle with Not Started , In Progress , and Completed statuses, as shown in Figure 9.12. By default, the process steps start with Not Started and move to In Progress either when the process step owner manually changes the status or when the automation criteria is satisfied and the © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 339 background automation technical job moves the status to In Progress . For example, the product review step is configured to start on the start date of January 1 at 9 a.m. When this date and time criteria are reached, the system automatically moves the status to In Progress . The status completions are reached either by the process step owner manually changing the status or when the automation criteria are reached; for example, the demand review step is set to Complete when all the tasks are completed. If all the tasks are completed, the progress moves to 100%.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Figure 9.12 Process and Process Step Status Lifecycle There are a few secondary exception statuses that can be defined by the process template owner for certain automation criteria. For example, when the start date is reached and the previous step isn’t completed, the step stays in Not Started status with a secondary user defined with the status of Delayed . Similarly, when the end date of the step is reached and the step isn’t completed, perhaps because the tasks associated with the step aren’t completed, then the step is still in In Progress status with a secondary status of Overdue .

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: As stated earlier, the process step owner can manually change the status as required, which will override the automation criteria set for the step. Only the process step owner or the process owner has the authority to change the status of the process step. The process step uses the permission filters of the process step owner, which means that any application job scheduled as part of the process step will run with the process step owner’s permission filters. This ensures that the jobs are run with the right authorizations.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: In addition, the background process automation job will schedule the application jobs using the permission filters of the process step owner. As shown in Figure 9.13, the process step owner can manage the lifecycle of the process step within the Manage Process app or from the process chart in the SAP IBP dashboard. Depending on the status of the current process step, the next Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 340 possible step status is shown for the process step owner to change the status of the step. Figure 9.13 Manage Process Lifecycle Status When a step is set to In Progress , the following set of activities happens: 1. Tasks are assigned to participant groups or users. 2. Task notification emails are sent out by SAP Build Work Zone. 3. If there are any application jobs associated with the start step, they’re triggered immediately. 4. If there are any custom alert subscriptions associated with the start step, they are executed. 5.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: As users complete the tasks, the progress of the process increases. 6. Once all tasks are completed, the process step progress reaches 100%, and the step moves to Completed status based on the automation criteria defined for the step. For example, if automation is set to end when all tasks are completed, then the step is set to the Completed status once all tasks are finished. If automation is based on the end date and task completion, then the step goes to Completed status when the end date is reached and the tasks are completed. 7.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: If there are any application jobs associated with the end of the step, they’re started. 8. If there are any custom alert subscriptions associated with the end step, they are executed. © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 341 Further details about task management will be covered in Section 9.4. 9.3.4 Monitoring Process Status The Manage Processes app provides nice visualizations and better usability to quickly get to the information that is most relevant for finding bottlenecks in the process. The visualization and monitoring aspects of the process include the following: Status of each process step Progress percentage of each step Gantt chart view of processes and tasks View status of application job runs and navigate to application job View custom alert counts and navigate to custom alerts for the alert details View task completion status for participants Navigation to SAP Build Work Zone collaboration workspace for further collaboration The Gantt chart view of the process gives a quick visual indication of the progress of the process steps, timelines, and associated tasks with their statuses.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: As an example, the monthly S&OP process for Mexico is shown in Figure 9.14. The Demand Review step is overdue and the step is only 67% complete, with two out of the three tasks completed. The reason for this, as shown in Figure 9.14, is that the Run Statistical Forecasting task hasn’t been completed. Figure 9.14 Gantt Chart View of Process Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 342 Because of this, the next step, Supply Review , isn’t started because it’s dependent on the completion of the demand review step, so its secondary status is set to Delayed , as shown in Figure 9.15. Figure 9.15 Process Step with Delayed Status In this case, the second step will resume processing as soon as the first step is set to Complete , either by manually completing the process step or automatically when the last task associated with the step is completed. It’s clear that because of a delay in one step, the consecutive steps are a ff ected, especially if they have dependencies.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: This is made transparent to the planner and the planner can take necessary steps to either readjust the dates of the dependent steps or let the process continue with the reduced duration. 9.3.5 Process Dashboards In addition to the list view in the Manage Processes app, where multiple processes can be viewed together, the Dashboard app in SAP IBP provides the functionality to add process-related charts together with other analytical charts, thereby showing the process- and data-related charts together in one view. This also o ff ers the ability to view multiple processes together based on user selection criteria.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: You can select any open/running processes and include them in the dashboard. For example, all the running processes can be included in a process dashboard along with other analytical charts, such as consensus revenue per month, as shown in Figure 9.16. © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 343 Figure 9.16 View Multiple Processes in the Dashboard In SAP IBP dashboards, users can choose to include analytical charts, alerts, and process charts. The controls on the process chart in the dashboard also now provide options to swap the process chart with another chart. The process chart in the process dashboard is interactive, in the sense that you can select di ff erent process steps to see the step details and tasks. The process charts display a chevron of the process steps with their statuses and completion percentages.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: For each process step, the step details, process participation, task assignments, and completions are displayed, along with navigation to SAP Build Work Zone workspaces, application jobs, custom alerts, and tasks. By default, the running process step for a process is shown in the chart. Similar to the Manage Process app, the lifecycle of a process step can be managed from the process chart by setting the step to In Progress or Completed . The Tasks list shows the status for each task associated with the step. If there are tasks that are falling behind, overdue email notifications can be sent directly from the process chart, as shown in Figure 9.17.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 344 Figure 9.17 Tasks Notification Email for Delayed Tasks SAP Best Practices for Process Management A tips and tricks document titled “Process Management for Unified Planning Process” is available as part of SAP Best Practice content. It describes the process orchestration within and between processes carried out, for example, in S&OP by a sales and operations coordinator, in demand planning by a demand planner, and so on. This illustrates an overall orchestration layer for the unified planning process and how integration points between the SAP IBP applications will be automated as much as possible. © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 345 9.4 Task Management To manage workflow of tasks, SAP IBP process management provides the necessary functionality to create task templates, task assignments, notifications, completions from the web UI and Excel UI, and task monitoring. SAP IBP tasks are realized as SAP Build Work Zone tasks. Further, if you don’t have an SAP Build Work Zone environment, then tasks management can be handled by SAP IBP. You can further create nonprocess-related tasks from the new Manage Tasks app. SAP IBP task management provides automated task assignment with notifications and progress monitoring, where the following occurs: Define default tasks for each process step and assign to participants groups and users.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Tasks are automatically generated and assigned when the process is set to In Progress . Task email notifications are sent out to the users. Tasks can be completed from the Manage Tasks app; in the SAP Integrated Business Planning, add-in for Microsoft Excel; in SAP Build Work Zone; or directly from Process Step Details in the Manage Processes app. Tasks can be monitored in the Manage Tasks, Process Dashboards, or Manage Processes apps. As tasks are completed, the process progress increases. Planners like to be notified when they have a task and be able to finish the tasks assigned to them easily without navigation to multiple screens.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: This section covers details about how tasks are created, assigned, and completed in SAP IBP. We’ll also cover how task completions can be performed from SAP Integrated Business Planning, add-in for Microsoft Excel, and finally we’ll cover how the process progresses to the next stage of completion for the tasks. 9.4.1 Tasks Assignments and Completions Tasks are created for each process step in a process template with assignments to process step participant groups and/or users, as follows: Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 346 1. When a step is set to In Progress , SAP Build Work Zone tasks are created for each user assigned to the step. If the user isn’t yet part of the SAP Build Work Zone workspace, an invitation to join the workspace is sent first. 2. A notification email is sent from SAP Build Work Zone to users about the task assignment and due date. 3. To facilitate ad hoc tasks beyond the standard tasks in the template, the Manage Tasks app lets users create ad hoc tasks and assign them to users in the process step along with due dates.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: In addition, users can assign a task to be tracked in the process step progress percentage, as shown in Figure 9.18. 4. When logged in to SAP IBP, whether from the web UI or Excel, users can view their open tasks and complete them. In the web UI, there is an app called Manage Tasks. In this app, the open tasks for the logged-in user are displayed. The user can complete the tasks directly from here or navigate to SAP Build Work Zone tasks and complete them from there. 5. When a user is logged in through Excel, the SAP IBP tab will show a Tasks area that lists open tasks; the user can view and complete tasks from there. 6.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: After a user completes a task, the process step progress increases accordingly. For example, say there are four tasks for users assigned. If one of the users completes a task, the step progress increases to 25%. 7. When all the tasks are completed, the process step reaches 100% and then can be set to Completed automatically if the step completion criteria are reached. 8. Users participating in a process can view the status of the process step and the tasks completion in the Manage Process app to see who has completed a task on time and who has fallen behind schedule. 9.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: In SAP Build Work Zone, further information can be gathered or collaboration can be done for each task. For example, you may want to attach documents to the task. New ad hoc tasks can be created from SAP Build Work Zone that aren’t part of SAP IBP process management. © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 347 Figure 9.18 Create Ad Hoc Tasks for Process Reminders for automated tasks from process management can be shown for a user as notifications on the SAP Fiori launchpad. The task reminders are sent to users who have open tasks n days (configured in the process step) before the end date of the process step is approaching. 9.4.2 Tasks Completion from SAP Integrated Business Planning, Add-In for Microsoft Excel SAP Integrated Business Planning, add-in for Microsoft Excel, provides the functionality to view and complete tasks from Excel.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: When a user is participating in an S&OP process—such as a demand planner as part of a demand review step currently in progress—they are notified in the Tasks group of the SAP IBP tab about the number of open tasks, as shown in Figure 9.19. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 348 Figure 9.19 Task Management in SAP Integrated Business Planning, Add-In for Microsoft Excel This demand planner can then click on the Tasks icon to see the list of open tasks, which can be grouped by Due Date , Priority , or Process . When grouped by Process , the Tasks screen will show all the open tasks across di ff erent processes to which the user is assigned. When the user selects the information context of the task, it will display the task details along with the details of process steps and the progress percentage.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: In Figure 9.19, the Demand Review Meeting task is open for this planner and is due, as indicated in red. The progress is 67%, with two out of three tasks completed; when the user completes this activity, the progress of the process step will reach 100%. The demand planner can then perform his final steps, which could include making some planning data changes and/or setting up the demand review meeting and marking the task as Completed directly from Excel. 9.4.3 Process Progress Based on Tasks Completion When the demand planner completes this task from Excel or the Manage Tasks app, and when all tasks associated with the process step are completed, the Demand Review process step immediately goes to Completed status.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Consequently, the following step, Supply Review , which is dependent on completion of the Demand Review step, goes to In Progress status. As shown in Figure 9.20, the Demand Review step is at 100% and is set to Completed . The end application job associated with Demand Review —a copy operator to copy final demand to consensus demand for supply planning—is triggered. The Supply Review step goes into In Progress status, and tasks are created for the users participating in this step. As shown in Figure 9.20, the progress of the Supply Review keeps increasing as tasks are completed by end users. © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 349 Figure 9.20 Automation of Process Step Based on Task Completion Thus, process management provides transparency into the process steps that need attention; when the process blockers are handled, the process automatically moves to the next steps. If the supply review step has a delay, it’s captured in the status of the step, and such information will be useful in future releases of SAP IBP, in which process adherence key performance indicators (KPIs) are planned to be tracked, giving process owners the ability to see process improvements over time, process participation, process-to-process comparisons, and so on.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Upon completion of all the steps associated with the process, the process is closed automatically and appears under Closed Processes , as shown in Figure 9.21. Figure 9.21 Process List View of Completed Processes Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

SAP Build Work Zone provides a customizable digital workplace solution for users and is a unified entry point to centralized information, collaboration, and business applications. An SAP Build Work Zone workspace can be assigned to each process step to provide collaboration across several cross-functional teams. For our example process, you could create an SAP Build Work Zone collaboration workspace for each process step, as shown in Table 9.2.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP

When the process step starts, the participant users who are assigned tasks are automatically sent an invitation to join the SAP Build Work Zone workspace. Additional users can be added directly to the SAP Build Work Zone workspace who may or may not be part of the process. docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 351 Zone workspace for demand review, which enables collaboration among participants of the demand review process step. SAP IBP uses SAP Build Work Zone for task assignments, as we covered in detail in Section 9.4. Figure 9.22 SAP Build Work Zone Workspace for Demand Review Note The process management functionality will work even if you don’t have SAP Build Work Zone enabled, except for the collaboration aspects and decision- making tools that are dependent on SAP Build Work Zone. docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 352 9.6 Application Programming Interfaces for Process Management SAP IBP provides the following APIs for reporting and triggering process management externally: APIs for external reporting of process status, tasks completions, process improvements over time APIs to externally trigger create, delete processes, change status of process steps To improve visibility, transparency, and adherence to a process, you can report on process data using the API provided for process management. You can extract various process management–related data for external reporting on information about the processes, individual steps, tasks, or other details on the process-step level.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: Using this information, you can keep track of all or specific processes with respect to tasks that are due or any approaching deadlines. A new OData V4 service /IBP/API_PROCMGMT_MANAGE , along with the setup of a communication arrangement based on the new Planning - Process Management ( SAP_COM_0749 ) communication scenario, enables you to extract information about processes from SAP IBP. To externally trigger SAP IBP process management, you can use the same OData V4 service /IBP/API_PROCMGMT_MANAGE . This will enable you to manage planning processes in SAP IBP with an external tool.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: For example, you can trigger monthly S&OP process automation from an external scheduler after data loads are completed. For more information about how to use the service, see SAP Note 3033483. © 2026 by Rheinwerk Publishing Inc., Boston (MA)

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: 353 9.7 Summary In this chapter, we covered details of how to create and run an S&OP process using process management capabilities in SAP Integrated Business Planning for sales and operations. We also detailed setting up process templates with process step roles, durations, task assignments, automation criteria, alerts, and orchestration of application jobs. We then covered how to manage and run recurring processes, including creating a process, managing the process lifecycle, monitoring the status of the process steps and exception conditions, and using process charts and dashboards to view and manage multiple running processes.

docs.bookTitle: Sales and Operations Planning with SAP IBP
docs.text: We next covered details of task assignments and completions, along with how planners can easily complete tasks in Excel and how process steps can progress upon completion of tasks. We finally covered how SAP Build Work Zone collaboration and process management are seamlessly integrated. All these capabilities provide robust process orchestration and management of processes across cross-functional organization units, providing transparency, visibility, and adherence to the process.
